topics.title: Alphabet & Sounds
topics.description: The Spanish alphabet, ñ, accents, and tricky sounds

guide.intro: Spanish uses the Latin alphabet plus one extra letter — ñ — and a small set of accent marks. The good news: Spanish spelling is highly phonetic, so once you know the rules, you can read almost any word out loud.

sections.text: 27 letters
Spanish has the 26 English letters plus ñ (eñe). The letters CH and LL used to count as separate letters but are now treated as digraphs.
Vowels — only 5 sounds
Spanish vowels each have exactly one sound, no matter the word. Unlike English where 'a' can sound like in 'cat', 'father', or 'about', Spanish 'a' is always 'ah'.
The letter ñ
ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon'. It's a completely separate letter — año (year) and ano (anus) are different words, so the tilde matters!
The rolled R
Single 'r' between vowels is a soft flap (like the 't' in American 'butter'). Double 'rr' or 'r' at the start of a word is a strong trill — practice by purring like a cat.
J and soft G
Spanish 'j' is like a strong English 'h' (from the back of the throat). Spanish 'g' before e or i sounds the same — so 'gente' and 'jefe' both start with that throaty sound.
LL and Y
LL is pronounced like English 'y' in most regions (in Argentina it sounds like 'sh'). Y by itself is also 'ee' and means 'and'.
Accent marks (´)
The accent does two things: it shows which syllable to stress, and it distinguishes word pairs that are otherwise spelled identically.
¿ and ¡
Spanish opens questions with an upside-down ¿ and exclamations with ¡. They tell the reader the tone from the very first word, since Spanish word order doesn't always change in questions.
On a US keyboard, get ¿ with Option+Shift+? and ¡ with Option+1 (Mac), or use Alt codes / character shortcuts on Windows.

exercises.explanation: Spanish 'i' is always 'ee'. So 'sí' (yes) sounds exactly like English 'see'.

exercises.prompt: How does Spanish 'u' sound?
exercises.explanation: Spanish 'u' is always the 'oo' sound, like English 'food' or 'boot'.

exercises.explanation: c-A-s-A — two 'ah' sounds. Every Spanish vowel you see, you pronounce.

exercises.explanation: English unstressed vowels often become 'uh' (about → uh-bout). Spanish vowels stay pure.

exercises.explanation: a-i-r-e: three different vowels (a, i, e). 'casa' and 'mesa' have only 2 distinct vowels.

exercises.explanation: Before e/i, Spanish 'g' becomes throaty — same sound as 'j'. So 'gente' and a hypothetical 'jente' would sound the same.

topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Hello, goodbye, please, thank you — and the tú/usted distinction

guide.intro: Spanish greetings are warm and varied — and they have different forms depending on time of day and how formal you want to sound.

sections.text: Hello & goodbye
Note 'buenos' (días) is masculine plural, but 'buenas' (tardes/noches) is feminine plural. That's because día is masculine even though it ends in -a!
How are you?
Tú vs Usted

Spanish has two words for 'you' in the singular. Tú is informal — for friends, family, kids, peers. Usted is formal — for strangers, older people, customers, professional contexts. Usted takes the same verb endings as 'he/she' (él/ella).
In Spain, tú is used very widely — even with strangers in casual settings. In much of Latin America, usted is more common with anyone you don't know well. When in doubt, start with usted.
Please, thank you, sorry

topics.title: Subject Pronouns
topics.description: Yo, tú, él, ella — and why Spanish often drops them

guide.intro: Spanish has subject pronouns just like English — but it also has a superpower: it can drop them entirely. Because each verb form already shows who's doing the action, you usually don't need 'yo' or 'tú' at all.

sections.text: The full set

rows: only used in Spain; Latin America uses ustedes
formal in Spain; standard 'you all' in Latin America

sections.text: Dropping subject pronouns

Spanish verb endings tell you the subject. 'Hablo español' literally means 'speak Spanish' — but the -o ending of 'hablo' already means 'I', so you don't need to say 'yo'. Native speakers usually drop the pronoun unless they want to emphasize the subject or clear up ambiguity.
Use the pronoun for contrast: 'Yo hablo español, él habla inglés' (I speak Spanish; HE speaks English). Otherwise, dropping is the natural choice.
Nosotros vs nosotras
Group pronouns have gender. Use -os for a group of all men or a mixed group. Use -as only when EVERY person in the group is female.
Vosotros vs Ustedes
For 'you all', Spain uses 'vosotros/vosotras' for friends and 'ustedes' for formal. Latin America has dropped 'vosotros' completely — 'ustedes' covers both informal and formal you-all.
If you're learning Latin American Spanish, focus on ustedes for all plural 'you'. Vosotros is rarely used outside Spain.

topics.title: Ser vs Estar
topics.description: Two verbs for 'to be' — the heart of Spanish

guide.intro: English has ONE verb for 'to be'. Spanish has TWO: ser and estar. They are not interchangeable. Picking the wrong one can change the meaning of a sentence — sometimes drastically. Get this right and the rest of A1 falls into place.

sections.text: The big idea
SER describes what something IS — identity, origin, profession, time, permanent traits. ESTAR describes how something IS RIGHT NOW — location, state, feeling, condition.

rows: Location (Estoy en casa — I'm at home)
Origin (Soy de Perú — I'm from Peru)
Temporary state (El café está caliente — The coffee is hot)
Time/date (Son las dos — It's two o'clock)

sections.text: Conjugations (present)
Tricky pairs — same English, different Spanish
Location uses ESTAR — even when the location is permanent! 'Madrid está en España' (Madrid is in Spain). The one exception: events use SER: 'La fiesta es en mi casa' (The party is at my house).
A handy mnemonic
SER → DOCTOR: Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship. ESTAR → PLACE: Position, Location, Action (ongoing), Condition, Emotion.

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Count from 1 to 100, ask prices, give your age

guide.intro: Spanish numbers follow mostly regular patterns — once you know 1–15 and the tens, you can build everything up to 99.

sections.text: 16–29: one word
16–29 fuse the ten + 'y' + digit into one word with a slight sound change: diez y seis → dieciséis.
30–99: tens + y + digit
From 30 onward, you write three words: ten + y (and) + digit. 'treinta y uno' = 31.
Uno → un / una
'uno' becomes 'un' before a masculine noun and 'una' before a feminine noun: un libro (one book), una mesa (one table), veintiún años (21 years — with accent!).
Age uses TENER
In Spanish, you HAVE years, you don't BE years. 'I am 25 years old' → 'Tengo 25 años' (I have 25 years). NEVER 'Soy 25.'

topics.title: Everyday Verbs
topics.description: Present tense: hablar, comer, vivir, ir, tener, hacer

guide.intro: Spanish verbs end in -ar, -er, or -ir. Each group has a regular set of present-tense endings. Learn the patterns, then you can conjugate hundreds of verbs.

sections.text: Regular -AR verbs (hablar — to speak)
Regular -ER verbs (comer — to eat)
Regular -IR verbs (vivir — to live)
Notice that -ER and -IR endings only differ in the nosotros (-emos vs -imos) and vosotros (-éis vs -ís) forms. The other four forms are identical.
Irregular: IR (to go)
Irregular: TENER (to have)
Irregular: HACER (to do/make)

TENER is used for many things English uses 'to be' for: age (tengo 25 años), hunger (tengo hambre), thirst (tengo sed), cold (tengo frío), heat (tengo calor), fear (tengo miedo). Memorize 'tengo + X' patterns!

guide.intro: Every Spanish noun is either MASCULINE or FEMININE — even objects, ideas, and abstract things. The article and any adjectives must match the noun's gender. This is the second biggest source of English-speaker errors (after ser/estar).

sections.text: The four definite articles
Indefinite articles
'unos' / 'unas' mean 'some' or 'a few'.
Predicting gender
In general, nouns ending in -O are masculine and nouns ending in -A are feminine. But there are important exceptions you should learn early.

rows: el libro, el perro, el carro
la mesa, la casa, la chica
el problema, el tema, el programa
el día (day), el mapa (map), el agua*

sections.text: 'agua' is feminine but uses 'el' in the singular (el agua) because Spanish avoids 'la a-' sound clash. Plural goes back to feminine: las aguas. Adjectives stay feminine: el agua fría.
Why does it matter?
Adjectives must match. 'A red car' = un carro rojo (masc) but 'a red house' = una casa roja (fem). Possessives mostly don't care (mi libro, mi mesa), but nuestro/nuestra and adjectives do.
Learn the article WITH the noun. Don't memorize 'libro' — memorize 'el libro'. This saves you from gender mistakes later.

topics.title: Questions
topics.description: Quién, qué, dónde, cuándo, cómo, por qué

guide.intro: Question words in Spanish are surprisingly close to English question words. The biggest news: question words ALWAYS take an accent, even when they look the same as a non-question version of the word.

sections.text: The question words
All question words carry a written accent. 'que' (without accent) = 'that, which'; 'qué' (with accent) = 'what?'. Same letters, different meaning.
No 'do/does' helper
English uses 'do/does' to form questions ('Do you live here?'). Spanish doesn't. Just put the verb after the question word — or just raise intonation for yes/no questions.
Por qué vs porque
¿Por qué? (two words, with accent) = 'why?'. Porque (one word, no accent) = 'because'. Question vs answer.
Qué vs Cuál
'¿Qué…?' usually asks for a definition or identification ('What is X?'). '¿Cuál…?' asks 'which one?' from a known set.

topics.title: Colors & Adjectives
topics.description: Colors plus the rules of adjective agreement and position

guide.intro: Colors are great vocabulary AND great practice for the two big adjective rules: agreement (gender and number) and position (usually after the noun).

sections.text: Core colors
Two rules to memorize
1) Agreement: Adjectives must match the noun in gender and number. 2) Position: Spanish adjectives normally come AFTER the noun, not before.
NEVER 'rojo carro'. Spanish puts color/quality adjectives AFTER the noun. (A handful of adjectives — bueno, gran, otro — can go before, but colors don't.)
Adjectives ending in -e or consonant
Adjectives ending in -e (verde, grande, azul, gris) have no separate masculine/feminine form. They only change for number: añade -s if it ends in a vowel, -es if it ends in a consonant.

topics.title: Weather
topics.description: Hace sol, llueve, hace frío — and 'tener frío' for people

guide.intro: Spanish describes weather in three patterns: 'hace' + noun (it makes...), 'está' + adjective (it is...), and individual verbs (llueve, nieva). And remember: people don't BE cold — people HAVE cold.

sections.text: HACE + noun (most common)
For most weather, use the impersonal 'hace' (from hacer = to make) plus a noun. Literally 'it makes sun', 'it makes cold'.
ESTÁ + adjective
For some conditions, use 'está' + adjective.
Single verbs
People: TENER frío/calor
For people, use TENER, not estar. 'I'm cold' = 'Tengo frío' (I have cold). 'I'm hot' = 'Tengo calor'. Never 'soy frío' or 'estoy caliente'! ('Estoy caliente' has a sexual meaning — be careful.)
Seasons

topics.title: Places & Location
topics.description: En casa, al parque — using 'en' for in/on/at

guide.intro: Spanish uses 'en' for what English splits into 'in', 'on', and 'at'. Location uses estar. 'a' is the destination word: 'voy a casa' (I go home).

sections.text: Places vocabulary
'En' = in / on / at
Spanish 'en' covers a lot of English prepositions. 'estoy en casa' = I'm at home / in the house. 'en la mesa' = on the table. 'en Madrid' = in Madrid.

rows.source: El libro está en la mesa
rows.translation: The book is on the table

sections.text: 'A' = to (destination)
When you GO somewhere, use 'a'. Verbs of motion (ir, viajar, llegar) take 'a' before the destination.
a + el → al (contraction). a + la → a la (no contraction). de + el → del. Memorize these tiny shortcuts.
Location uses ESTAR
Where something IS = estar, even when permanent. 'Madrid está en España' — Madrid is in Spain.
Useful location words

items: SER for identity / origin / profession / time / permanent traits

levels.description: Tell stories in the past, talk about what you used to do, order food, go shopping, and make plans.

topics.title: The preterite — what you did
topics.description: Talk about finished actions: 'I ate', 'we went', 'she said'.

guide.intro: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) is Spanish's main 'simple past' tense. You use it for actions that started and finished at a specific point — 'I called her yesterday', 'we ate at eight'.

sections.text: Regular endings
Drop the -ar/-er/-ir and add these endings. Notice the stress marks on the yo and él forms — they're load-bearing.

rows.source: hablar → hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron
rows.translation: I spoke, you spoke, he/she spoke, we spoke, you (pl.) spoke, they spoke

rows.source: comer → comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
rows.translation: I ate, you ate, he/she ate, we ate, you (pl.) ate, they ate

rows.source: vivir → viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
rows.translation: I lived, you lived, he/she lived, we lived, you (pl.) lived, they lived

sections.text: The big four irregulars
Four verbs you'll use constantly have irregular preterites. Memorize them — they don't follow the rules.

rows.source: ser / ir → fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
rows.translation: I was / I went (yes, same forms for both!)

rows.source: hacer → hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
rows.translation: to do/make — 'hizo' has a z, not c

rows.source: decir → dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron
ver → vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron
rows.translation: to see — no accents on 'vi' or 'vio'

sections.text: Time markers that scream 'preterite': ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado, en 2010, una vez.

topics.description: Talk about habits, ongoing scenes, and 'when I was a kid…'.

guide.intro: The imperfect (pretérito imperfecto) is the past for things without a clear end: routines, ongoing states, descriptions, ages, weather, and feelings in the past.

sections.text: Regular endings — only two patterns

rows.source: hablar → hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban
rows.translation: I used to speak / I was speaking

rows.source: comer → comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían
rows.translation: I used to eat / I was eating

rows.source: vivir → vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivíais, vivían
rows.translation: I used to live / I was living

sections.text: All -er and -ir verbs share one set of endings (-ía). That makes the imperfect easier than the preterite.
The only three irregulars

rows.source: ser → era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran
rows.translation: I was, you were, he/she was…

rows.source: ir → iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban
rows.translation: I used to go / I was going

rows.source: ver → veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían
rows.translation: I used to see / I was seeing

sections.text: When to reach for it

Use the imperfect for: (a) habits — 'every Sunday we ate paella'; (b) ongoing background — 'it was raining'; (c) age, time, weather in the past — 'tenía diez años', 'eran las tres'; (d) feelings/states — 'estaba cansado'.
English clue words: 'used to', 'would (often)', 'was/were -ing'. If you can rewrite a sentence with one of those, you almost always want the imperfect.

topics.title: Preterite vs imperfect — the big choice
topics.description: When to use which past. The single most useful skill at A2.

guide.intro: Spanish forces a choice English doesn't: was the past action a finished event (preterite) or an ongoing scene/habit (imperfect)? Same English sentence often maps to either, depending on what you mean.

sections.text: The mental test
Ask yourself: 'Could I add WHEN this happened (a specific time)?' If yes → preterite. 'Was this the background, what was going on, what used to happen?' → imperfect.

rows.translation: Yesterday I ate pizza. (one event, finished)

rows.source: De niño, comía pizza todos los viernes.
rows.translation: As a kid I used to eat pizza every Friday. (habit)
I was eating pizza when you called me. (ongoing + interrupting event)

sections.text: The classic combo: imperfect + preterite
When something interrupts an ongoing scene, Spanish uses BOTH tenses in one sentence: the scene is imperfect, the interruption is preterite.

rows.source: Yo dormía cuando sonó el teléfono.
rows.translation: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

rows.source: Veíamos la tele cuando llegó mi padre.
rows.translation: We were watching TV when my father arrived.

sections.text: Trigger words

rows.source: Preterite triggers: ayer, anoche, el lunes, una vez, de repente, en 2010.

sections.text: Same verb, different meaning depending on tense: 'conocí a María' = I met María (for the first time); 'conocía a María' = I knew María (already).

topics.description: me ducho, te llamas, se levanta — verbs that loop back on yourself.

guide.intro: Reflexive verbs end in -se in the dictionary (lavarse, ducharse, llamarse) and need a matching pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) before a conjugated verb. They're routine in Spanish for things you do to yourself.

topics.title: Object pronouns — lo, la, le, les
topics.description: Replace nouns with pronouns: 'Lo veo' = 'I see it'.

guide.intro: English says 'I see John' → 'I see him'. Spanish does the same swap — but the pronoun goes BEFORE the conjugated verb, not after. 'Veo a Juan' → 'Lo veo'.

sections.text: Direct object pronouns

rows.source: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las
rows.translation: me, you, him/it, her/it, us, you (pl.), them (m.), them (f.)
I see Juan. → I see him.
I buy the shirt. → I buy it.

sections.text: Indirect object pronouns
These mark 'to/for whom'. Forms: me, te, le, nos, os, les. Same as direct except 3rd person uses 'le/les' (no gender).

rows.source: Le doy el libro a María.
rows.translation: I give the book to María.

sections.text: Placement rule
Before a conjugated verb: 'Lo veo'. Attached to an infinitive or -ndo form: 'Voy a verlo' / 'Estoy viéndolo'. With negatives, 'no' stays at the very front: 'No lo veo'.
Never put the pronoun after a conjugated verb in normal sentences. 'Veo lo' is wrong — must be 'Lo veo'.

topics.title: The personal 'a'
topics.description: When Spanish requires the little word 'a' before a person: 'Veo a María', not 'Veo María'.

guide.intro: Spanish does something English never does: it puts the preposition 'a' before a direct object when that object is a specific person (or beloved animal). 'Veo a María' literally feels like 'I see to María', but it's just how Spanish marks animate, identifiable direct objects.

sections.text: The core rule
If your direct object is a specific, animate being — a named person, a family member, a friend, your pet — insert 'a' right before it. If the object is a thing, no 'a'.
Pets and beloved animals
If you treat the animal as an individual (your dog, the family cat), use 'a'. Anonymous animals or animals in general usually skip it.

rows.source: Paseo a mi perro todos los días.
rows.translation: I walk my dog every day.
At the zoo we saw elephants.

sections.text: The 'tener' exception
With 'tener' (to have) you usually drop the 'a', even with people. 'Tengo dos hermanos' — no 'a'. Same with indefinite, unspecified humans introduced by 'un/una': 'Necesito un médico' (any doctor).
Questions and relative clauses
Keep the 'a' even when it travels to the front of a question or sits before 'quien' in a relative clause.

rows.source: El hombre a quien conozco vive aquí.
rows.translation: The man whom I know lives here.

topics.title: The 'se' of unintentional action
topics.description: 'Se me cayó el vaso' — I dropped the glass... but Spanish makes it sound like the glass dropped itself.

guide.intro: When something goes wrong by accident, Spanish loves to deflect blame. Instead of 'I dropped the glass', a Spanish speaker often says 'Se me cayó el vaso' — literally 'the glass fell on me'. The accident has a victim (me, you, her…), not a culprit.

sections.text: The structure
The formula is: 'se + indirect-object pronoun + verb + subject'. The verb agrees with the thing that happened (the subject), not with the person to whom it happened.

rows.translation: I dropped the glass. (lit. 'the glass fell on me')
I forgot the birthday. (lit. 'the birthday slipped my mind')
He/she broke the phone. (lit. 'the phone broke on him/her')

sections.text: Plural subjects
When more than one thing did the dropping/breaking/getting-lost, the verb goes plural. The indirect pronoun stays the same.
All the indirect pronouns
Swap 'me' for 'te / le / nos / os / les' to change whose accident it is.
Common verbs in this pattern
Caer (to fall/drop), olvidar (to forget), romper (to break), perder (to lose), quemar (to burn), escapar (to escape), ocurrir (to occur).
Use 'Se me cayó' when it was an accident. If you smashed it on purpose, use the active voice: 'Rompí el vaso'.

topics.title: Reflexive verbs that aren't reflexive
topics.description: Why 'me voy' isn't 'I go to myself' — when 'se' adds emphasis, not reflection.

guide.intro: Many Spanish verbs come in two flavors: a plain form and a 'se' form. The reflexive pronoun isn't always about doing something to yourself — sometimes it just emphasizes completion, surprise, or a change of state. Knowing the difference is what separates beginners from intermediate speakers.

sections.text: ir vs irse
'Ir' is about destination ('I'm going to the bank'). 'Irse' is about leaving where you are ('I'm leaving / I'm out of here').
dormir vs dormirse
'Dormir' is to sleep (a state). 'Dormirse' is to fall asleep (the moment you cross over).

rows.translation: I fell asleep on the couch.

sections.text: comer vs comerse
'Comer' is to eat. Adding 'se' adds emphasis: ate it all up, ate the whole thing.

rows.translation: I ate the whole pizza (all of it).

sections.text: morir vs morirse
'Morir' tends to be neutral/formal (deaths in news, in battle). 'Morirse' carries emotional weight or accidental flavor — often used figuratively ('Me muero de risa' = I'm dying of laughter).

rows.source: Se murió mi abuelo el año pasado.

sections.text: Quick test: if you can mentally add 'right up / all of it / fully' to the English, the Spanish probably wants 'se'.

topics.title: Discourse particles — sounding natural
topics.description: 'Pues', 'bueno', 'vale', 'oye', 'mira', 'claro' — the little words that glue Spanish conversation.

guide.intro: Listen to two Spanish speakers and you'll hear 'pues', 'bueno', 'vale', 'oye', 'mira' every few seconds. These tiny words don't really mean anything — they manage the conversation. Skip them and you sound like a textbook. Use them and you sound like a person.

sections.text: pues — well…
Use 'pues' to soften a response, fill a thinking gap, or open a sentence. Think of it as English 'well…' or 'so…'.
bueno — alright, OK
'Bueno' agrees, wraps up, or moves the conversation on. It's flexible: 'OK then', 'alright', 'so anyway'.
vale (Spain) / está bien (LatAm) — OK, got it
In Spain, 'vale' is the all-purpose 'OK'. In Latin America, you'll hear 'está bien', 'dale' (Argentina), 'órale' (Mexico) instead. Pick the one for your region.
oye / mira — hey, look
'Oye' (listen) and 'mira' (look) grab attention and soften requests or interruptions. Friendly, casual.

rows.translation: Look, I wanted to tell you something.

sections.text: vamos / claro — come on, of course
'Vamos' can mean 'let's go' but also 'come on, you know what I mean'. 'Claro' = of course, naturally, sure.

rows.translation: Come on, it's not that hard.

sections.text: Don't overdo it — sprinkle these like salt. Two or three per minute makes you sound native. Twelve makes you sound nervous.

topics.title: Present Perfect — he/has + participio
topics.description: Past events with present relevance (he comido, has visto)

guide.intro: Spanish present perfect is formed with HABER + past participle: 'he comido' (I have eaten). It looks just like English, but usage differs by region. In Spain, 'he comido pizza esta semana' is normal. In Latin America, you'll often hear preterite — 'comí pizza esta semana' — for the same idea.

sections.text: Formation: haber + participio
Regular participles
Irregular participles (memorize!)

Two confusions: (1) Spanish 'he' is unrelated to English 'he' — it means 'I have'. (2) The participle never changes — always 'comido', never 'comida' even with feminine subjects: 'María ha comido' not 'María ha comida'.
When to use it
Use it for: (a) life experiences (¿Has estado en México?), (b) actions in time periods still open (hoy, esta semana), (c) actions with present consequence (he perdido las llaves).

rows.source: Esta mañana he ido al gimnasio.
rows.translation: This morning I went to the gym.

sections.text: Spain vs Latin America
Spain uses present perfect liberally for anything today or recent. Latin America strongly prefers preterite. 'Hoy he ido al banco' (Spain) vs 'Hoy fui al banco' (LatAm) — same idea.
Time markers: ya (already), todavía no / aún no (not yet), nunca (never), alguna vez (ever), siempre (always), hoy (today), esta semana/mes/año, últimamente (lately).

topics.title: Present Subjunctive — the WEIRDO triggers
topics.description: Wishes, emotions, doubt, recommendations — the mood with no clean English equivalent

guide.intro: The subjunctive is THE B1 milestone. English barely uses it ('if I were you'); Spanish uses it constantly. Endings are a small set — the hard part is knowing WHEN. The trigger is in the FIRST clause: something subjective pushes the verb in the 'que' clause into the subjunctive.

sections.text: WEIRDO — the six triggers

rows: querer que, esperar que, desear que
me alegra que, me molesta que, me da pena que
es importante que, es necesario que, es bueno que
recomendar que, pedir que, sugerir que
no creo que, dudar que, no es verdad que

sections.text: Forming the present subjunctive
Take the YO form of present indicative, drop -o, add 'opposite' vowel endings: -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
Full conjugations
Irregular subjunctives
The clue 'que' is your friend. Structure: [Main clause with subjective trigger] + QUE + [different subject + subjunctive]. Same subject? Use infinitive instead.

rows.translation: I want to eat. (same subject → infinitive)
I want YOU to eat. (different subject → subjunctive)

rows.source: Espero que tengas un buen día.
rows.translation: I hope you have a good day.

sections.text: When you KNOW something is true, stay in indicative. When you express doubt, hope, emotion, or a wish about it, switch to subjunctive. 'Sé que viene' (fact) vs 'Espero que venga' (wish).

topics.title: The Conditional — 'would' in Spanish
topics.description: haría, comería, viviría — hypothetical and polite forms

guide.intro: Spanish has a clean, single-word conditional. Where English uses 'would + verb', Spanish glues -ía onto the infinitive. Two main jobs: (1) hypothetical situations and (2) softening for politeness ('could you?', 'would you mind?').

sections.text: Formation: infinitive + -ía endings
Take the WHOLE infinitive (don't drop -ar/-er/-ir) and add conditional endings. Same endings for all three conjugations.
Irregular stems (same as future tense)
Uses

rows.translation: If I had money, I would travel.

sections.text: Conditional is built-in polite. 'Quiero un café' (blunt) → 'Querría un café' / 'Me gustaría un café' (polite restaurant version).
Don't confuse conditional ('vendría' — would come) with imperfect ('venía' — used to come). Conditional always has -ría- somewhere.

topics.title: Ser vs Estar — meaning shifts
topics.description: Beyond A1: when the SAME adjective changes meaning

guide.intro: By B1 you know ser = essence, estar = state/location. The advanced twist: many adjectives have TWO meanings — one with ser, another with estar. 'Es aburrido' (boring/dull) vs 'Está aburrido' (bored right now). Classic English-speaker trap.

sections.text: Adjectives that change meaning
Examples — same adjective, two stories

rows.translation: My teacher is boring (a dull person).
I'm bored. Want to go to a movie?

sections.text: Tone & temporary states

Even outside dual-meaning adjectives, ser vs estar carries nuance. 'Es delgado' (he is thin — description). 'Está delgado' (he LOOKS thin — has lost weight). Estar often expresses 'looks/seems' or 'has become'.
Estar muerto/vivo: dead and alive both use ESTAR, even though death is permanent! Spanish treats them as states resulting from a change. 'Mi abuelo está muerto.'
Rule of thumb: 'feel/look/seem' → ESTAR. Unchanging classification → SER. Permanent label or current state?

topics.title: Direct & Indirect Object Pronouns
topics.description: me/te/lo/la/le and the famous 'se lo digo'

guide.intro: Spanish replaces noun objects with short pronouns. You already know some (me, te). At B1 we master DOUBLE pronouns: 'Se lo dije' = 'I told it to him/her'. The order is fixed (indirect + direct), and when both are third person, the indirect 'le/les' shape-shifts to 'se'.

sections.text: The two object families
Order: indirect THEN direct
When you use both, the indirect always goes first. 'Me lo das' = 'You give it to me.' (me = to me, lo = it).
The le → se rule
If BOTH pronouns are third-person (le/les + lo/la/los/las), the indirect 'le' or 'les' becomes 'SE' to avoid the awkward 'le lo'.

rows.translation: I gave it (fem.) to María as a gift.

sections.text: Placement
Object pronouns go BEFORE conjugated verbs and AFTER (attached to) infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative commands.

rows.translation: I'm going to tell you. (attached to infinitive)
I'm telling you (right now). (attached to gerund)
Tell it to me! (attached to affirmative command)
Don't tell it to me! (before negative command)

sections.text: When pronouns attach to verbs (infinitive, gerund, command), you often need to ADD a written accent to preserve the original stress: decir → decírmelo, diciendo → diciéndomelo, dime → dímelo.
When the order is reshuffled or you want extra clarity, you can ADD 'a + person' to clarify who 'se' refers to: 'Se lo dije A ELLA' = 'I told it TO HER.'

topics.title: Modals: poder, deber, tener que, hay que
topics.description: Can/must/have-to and their polite forms

guide.intro: Spanish modal verbs let you talk about possibility, obligation, and necessity. Unlike English ('can / must / should'), Spanish modals conjugate fully and combine with an infinitive: 'puedo ir' (I can go), 'tengo que estudiar' (I have to study).

sections.text: The core modals
Examples

rows.translation: I have to go to the doctor.
One has to arrive at 9. / We need to be there at 9.
He knows how to play the guitar.

rows.source: Suelo ir al gimnasio los lunes.
rows.translation: I usually go to the gym on Mondays.

sections.text: Softening with conditional
To make modals polite or softer, use the conditional form. 'Puedes' becomes 'podrías' (could you), 'debes' becomes 'deberías' (should — softer).
hay que vs tener que
'Hay que' is IMPERSONAL — it's true for everyone, no specific subject. 'Tener que' is personal — someone specific has to do it.

rows.translation: One has to eat to live.

sections.text: Spanish has NO direct 'must' for inference like English ('he must be tired'). Use 'deber de': 'Debe de estar cansado' = 'He must be tired (probably).' Native speakers often skip the 'de' in casual speech.

topics.title: Storytelling — preterite + imperfect + past perfect
topics.description: Telling a story in past: actions, scenes, and what had happened before

guide.intro: Spanish past tenses split work three ways: PRETERITE for completed actions (what HAPPENED next), IMPERFECT for description and ongoing context (what WAS GOING ON), and PAST PERFECT for things that HAD ALREADY HAPPENED before the story moment. Mastering this trio is what makes you sound natural in narrative.

sections.text: Quick refresher
Imperfect — the background

rows.translation: It was night and it was raining.

rows.source: Yo tenía 12 años. Vivíamos en Madrid.
rows.translation: I was 12. We were living in Madrid.

rows.source: Mi abuela siempre cocinaba los domingos.
rows.translation: My grandma always cooked on Sundays.

sections.text: Preterite — the events

rows.source: Llegué a casa a las ocho.

sections.text: Combining them
Imperfect SETS THE SCENE; preterite PUSHES THE STORY FORWARD. 'Estaba en casa cuando llamó' = 'I was at home (background) when she called (event)'.

rows.source: Cuando era niño, vivía en Barcelona.
rows.translation: When I was a kid (background), I lived in Barcelona.
I was eating when the phone rang.

rows.source: Hacía sol, así que decidimos ir a la playa.
rows.translation: It was sunny, so we decided to go to the beach.

sections.text: Past perfect — what HAD happened first
Use había + participle for an action that happened BEFORE the main story moment.

rows.translation: When I arrived, they had already had dinner.

rows.source: No reconocí la calle: habían construido un edificio nuevo.
rows.translation: I didn't recognize the street: they had built a new building.
I had never seen so much snow.

sections.text: Time markers that often signal IMPERFECT: 'mientras' (while), 'siempre' (always), 'todos los días' (every day), 'a menudo' (often), 'de niño' (as a kid). Markers for PRETERITE: 'ayer', 'el otro día', 'el año pasado', 'en 1990', 'una vez', 'de repente' (suddenly).

Spanish does NOT use the past perfect as freely as English. 'I had eaten when she arrived' usually maps fine to 'Había comido cuando llegó.' But 'I just ate' = 'Acabo de comer' (no past perfect needed).

topics.title: Neutral 'lo' — the abstract pronoun
topics.description: lo bueno, lo que pasa, lo de Pedro — making abstract nouns from adjectives and ideas

guide.intro: Spanish 'lo' is tiny but mighty. It turns adjectives into abstract nouns (lo bueno = 'the good part'), references whole ideas (Lo que dijo me sorprendió = 'What he said surprised me'), and lets you refer back to entire situations (No lo sé). Master 'lo' and your Spanish suddenly sounds much more natural.

rows: the good thing / the good part

sections.text: The adjective stays masculine singular — it's not modifying any noun, just turning into an abstract concept.
lo que → 'what' / 'the thing that'

sections.text: lo as neutral object pronoun
Use 'lo' to refer back to an entire idea, not a specific noun: No lo sé (I don't know it / that), Te lo prometo (I promise [you that]), Lo siento (I'm sorry [about it]).
Comparison trick: 'más X de lo que pensaba' = 'more X than I thought'. Use 'de lo que' (not 'que') when comparing with a clause: Es más difícil de lo que parece.

topics.title: Double object pronoun placement
topics.description: Where to put me/te/se/lo/la — before verbs, attached to infinitives, with accents

guide.intro: Spanish pronouns dance around verbs by precise rules. With two pronouns (indirect + direct), order is always indirect first, direct second: 'me lo', 'te lo', 'se lo'. They go BEFORE conjugated verbs (Te lo doy), but ATTACH to infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative imperatives — often adding a written accent (dárselo, dándomelo, ¡cómpramelo!). One quirk: 'le' + 'lo' becomes 'se lo' (never 'le lo').

sections.text: Order: indirect + direct, always
le → se before lo/la/los/las

rows.source: Les digo la verdad. → Se la digo.

sections.text: Placement: 3 options

rows: Voy a dártelo / Te lo voy a dar.
Estoy dándotelo / Te lo estoy dando.

sections.text: Written accents appear when you attach pronouns and the stress would otherwise shift: da → dámelo (accent preserves the stress on 'da'), decir → decírselo, dando → dándotelo.

topics.title: Subjunctive's soft uses — blessings & hedging
topics.description: Que tengas buen día, Ojalá venga, No creo que sea — the gentler subjunctive triggers

guide.intro: Beyond the classic WEIRDO triggers (wishes, emotions, impersonal, requests, doubt, ojalá), the subjunctive shows up in softer, more idiomatic ways: standalone blessings (Que tengas buen día), 'ojalá' for hopes, negation of belief verbs (No creo que sea verdad), and after probability adverbs. These are the phrases that make daily Spanish feel warm and natural.

sections.text: Standalone 'Que + subjunctive' — blessings & wishes

rows.translation: May it go well for you.

sections.text: Ojalá — hopes (present subj.) and regrets (past subj.)

sections.text: No es que + subjunctive — concessive hedging

rows.translation: It's not that I don't want to — I can't.

rows.translation: It's not that it's bad, it's just weird.

sections.text: Probability adverbs — mood depends on confidence
'A lo mejor' is special — it always takes indicative even though it means 'maybe'. The others let you choose mood based on how sure you are.

topics.title: Imperfect subjunctive
topics.description: Past triggers, polite quisiera, and second-conditional 'si' clauses

guide.intro: The imperfect subjunctive is the past-tense counterpart of the present subjunctive. It shows up whenever a subjunctive trigger sits in a past or conditional clause: 'Quería que vinieras', 'Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría'. Two endings exist — '-ara/-iera' and '-ase/-iese' — and they're 100% interchangeable; the '-ara/-iera' family wins in everyday speech.

sections.text: Formation — the third-person plural shortcut
Take the 'ellos' form of the preterite, drop '-ron', and add the imperfect-subjunctive endings. This works for every verb — regular, irregular, stem-changing, you name it.

rows.source: hablar → hablaron → hablara, hablaras, hablara, habláramos, hablarais, hablaran
comer → comieron → comiera, comieras, comiera, comiéramos, comierais, comieran
tener → tuvieron → tuviera, tuvieras, tuviera, tuviéramos, tuvierais, tuvieran
ir/ser → fueron → fuera, fueras, fuera, fuéramos, fuerais, fueran

sections.text: Trigger: past main clause + subjunctive trigger

Same triggers as the present subjunctive (querer que, dudar que, es necesario que, para que…) but with the main verb in preterite, imperfect, conditional, or pluperfect. The subordinate verb shifts to imperfect subjunctive.

rows.source: Quería que vinieras a la fiesta.
rows.translation: I wanted you to come to the party.
It was necessary that we studied more.
I asked him to help me.

sections.text: Polite 'quisiera'
'Quisiera' (imperfect subjunctive of 'querer') is the politest way to ask for something in Spanish — softer than 'quiero', warmer than 'querría'. Treat it as the fixed polite form: 'I would like…'

rows.source: Quisiéramos reservar una mesa para dos.
rows.translation: We'd like to book a table for two.

sections.text: Si + imperfect subjunctive — hypothetical

The classic 'second conditional': 'If I had X, I would do Y'. Si + imperfect subjunctive in the if-clause, conditional in the result clause. Never use present subjunctive after 'si' — it doesn't exist there.

rows.source: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría por el mundo.
rows.translation: If I had money, I'd travel the world.

rows.source: Si fueras más paciente, te iría mejor.
rows.translation: If you were more patient, things would go better for you.

sections.text: Beware: '-ara/-iera' is the past subjunctive, NOT the conditional. 'Viajara' ≠ 'viajaría'. The if-clause uses subjunctive; the result uses conditional.

lessons.title: Forming the imperfect subjunctive
lessons.description: Drop -ron from preterite, add -ra endings

exercises.prompt: How do you form the imperfect subjunctive of a verb?

exercises.answer: Take the 'ellos' preterite, drop -ron, add -ra endings
exercises.explanation: This shortcut works for EVERY verb in Spanish — regulars and irregulars alike.

exercises.explanation: Both 'ser' and 'ir' share the preterite 'fueron' — and therefore the imperfect subjunctive 'fuera/fueras/fuera/fuéramos/fuerais/fueran'.

She asked us to wait

exercises.explanation: Past trigger 'quería' + subjunctive trigger 'que' → imperfect subjunctive 'vinieras'.

exercises.explanation: Imperfect subjunctive 'yo' of 'tener': tuviera.

exercises.prompt: Which ending is NOT a valid imperfect subjunctive form?
exercises.explanation: '-ería' is conditional, not subjunctive. Imperfect subjunctive uses -ara/-iera (common) or -ase/-iese (literary).

exercises.explanation: Don't forget the accent on the antepenultimate vowel: fuéramos (or 'fuésemos').

topics.title: Conditional perfect
topics.description: Habría + participle for past hypotheticals, regret, and third-conditional 'si' clauses

guide.intro: The conditional perfect — 'habría + participle' — is Spanish's 'would have done' tense. Use it for past hypotheticals you didn't actually do: 'I would have gone, but I was sick'. It's the natural partner of the pluperfect subjunctive in third-conditional 'si' clauses.

sections.text: Formation: habría + past participle
Conditional of 'haber' (habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían) + the past participle of the main verb. Participles don't agree — they always end in -o.

rows.translation: they would have told the truth

sections.text: Third conditional — si + pluperfect subj. + conditional perfect
Past unreal: 'If I had X-ed, I would have Y-ed'. The if-clause uses pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle); the result clause uses conditional perfect (habría + participle).

rows.translation: If I had known, I would have come.

rows.source: Si hubieras estudiado más, habrías aprobado.
rows.translation: If you had studied more, you would have passed.

sections.text: Regret and missed opportunity
Conditional perfect is the regret tense. Pair with 'pero' (but) to explain why the action didn't happen.

rows.source: Habría ido a la fiesta, pero estaba enfermo.
rows.translation: I would have gone to the party, but I was sick.

rows.source: Te lo habría dicho, pero no quería preocuparte.
rows.translation: I would have told you, but I didn't want to worry you.

sections.text: Irregular participles
Don't insert anything between 'haber' and the participle. 'Habría ya comido' is wrong — say 'Ya habría comido' or 'Habría comido ya'.

topics.title: Pluperfect (había + participle)
topics.description: Past-before-past in narration and reported speech

guide.intro: The pluperfect — 'había + participle' — is Spanish's 'had done' tense. Use it for the past-before-the-past: actions that happened before another past moment. 'When you called, I had already eaten' → 'Cuando llamaste, yo ya había comido.'

sections.text: Formation
Imperfect of 'haber' (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían) + past participle. Same family of irregular participles as the perfect tenses.

rows.translation: I had already eaten when you arrived.
We had never seen anything like it.
Had you been to Spain before?

sections.text: Sequence in storytelling
When telling a story in the past, the pluperfect drops in to mark something that happened EARLIER than the main timeline. Often paired with 'ya', 'todavía no', 'antes', 'cuando'.

rows.source: Cuando llegó el camarero, ya habíamos pedido.
rows.translation: When the waiter arrived, we had already ordered.

rows.source: No quería ir al cine porque ya había visto la película.
rows.translation: She didn't want to go to the cinema because she had already seen the film.

sections.text: Pluperfect vs preterite vs imperfect
Use preterite for completed past actions, imperfect for background/habits, pluperfect for past-before-past. The three often appear together in narration.

rows.source: Llegué tarde porque había perdido el autobús.
rows.translation: I arrived late because I had missed the bus.

rows.source: Estaba cansado porque no había dormido nada.
rows.translation: He was tired because he hadn't slept at all.

sections.text: English sometimes uses simple past where Spanish prefers pluperfect. 'I told him I saw it' often becomes 'Le dije que lo había visto' in Spanish.

topics.title: Passive voice
topics.description: Ser-passive (formal/news) vs se-passive (natural Spanish) vs impersonal se

guide.intro: Spanish has two passive flavors. The 'ser + participle' passive ('La casa fue construida en 1850') sounds formal — common in journalism. The 'se + verb' passive ('Se construyen muchas casas aquí') is what natives reach for in everyday speech. Master both, and lean on 'se' more often than not.

sections.text: Ser + participle (passive formal)
Like English: subject + ser (conjugated) + participle (agrees in gender/number) + por + agent. Mostly used in writing and news.

rows.source: El libro fue escrito por García Márquez.
rows.translation: The book was written by García Márquez.

rows.source: Las casas son construidas por la empresa local.
rows.translation: The houses are built by the local company.
The agreement will be signed tomorrow.

sections.text: Se + verb (passive 'se')
Most common in spoken Spanish. 'Se' goes before a verb in 3rd person; the verb agrees with the patient (the thing acted on).

rows.source: Se construyeron muchas casas el año pasado.
rows.translation: Many houses were built last year.

sections.text: Impersonal 'se' (no specific subject)
When you don't want to name a doer at all — 'one', 'people', 'they' — Spanish uses 'se + 3rd singular'. Useful for signs, recipes, instructions.

rows.translation: How do you say 'hello' in Spanish?

sections.text: Quick rule of thumb: if the subject is concrete and you'd just say 'X happened' without caring who did it, use se-passive. Reserve ser-passive for news headlines and formal writing.

items: Se alquila piso — Flat for rent
Se prohíbe pisar el césped — Keep off the grass

topics.title: Expressing opinions
topics.description: Hedge, agree, push back; master indicative/subjunctive triggers

guide.intro: B2 opinion-talk hinges on one rule: doubt and denial trigger subjunctive; certainty doesn't. 'Creo que es verdad' (indicative — I think it's true) vs 'No creo que sea verdad' (subjunctive — I don't think it's true). Master the trigger list, then layer in hedges and counterpoints.

sections.text: Indicative — when you're sure
Affirmative verbs of opinion and certainty take indicative: creo que, pienso que, opino que, estoy seguro de que, es verdad que, es cierto que.

rows.translation: It's true it rains a lot.

sections.text: Subjunctive — when you doubt or deny
Negative versions of those verbs and any expression of doubt, probability, or denial flip to subjunctive: no creo que, dudo que, es probable que, no es cierto que.

rows.source: No es cierto que sea tan caro.
rows.translation: It isn't true that it's that expensive.

sections.text: Hedge openers
B2 speakers pad opinions with hedges before committing: 'desde mi punto de vista', 'a mi parecer', 'en mi opinión', 'según yo'. These all take indicative in the dependent clause.

rows.source: Desde mi punto de vista, es un error.
rows.translation: From my point of view, it's a mistake.

rows.source: A mi parecer, no es tan grave.
rows.translation: To my mind, it's not that bad.

sections.text: Agreeing and pushing back

items: No estoy de acuerdo — I don't agree
No tengo claro que… — I'm not sure that… (+ subjunctive!)

sections.text: Question form flips back: '¿Crees que sea verdad?' (subjunctive — doubt embedded) vs '¿Crees que es verdad?' (indicative — neutral question). Many speakers use indicative both ways; subjunctive sounds slightly more doubtful.

guide.intro: Spanish news has its own register: short, dense headlines (often verbless), heavy use of ser-passive, and a stack of attribution phrases ('según fuentes', 'se rumorea', 'al parecer'). Read a few headlines a week and the patterns become second nature.

sections.text: Headline grammar
Spanish headlines often drop the verb of being, leaving a participle + noun: 'Detenidos tres sospechosos', 'Aprobada nueva ley'. Tight, eye-catching, and instantly recognizable as news.

rows.source: Aprobada la nueva ley de educación
Heridos dos en accidente de tráfico

sections.text: Attribution phrases
When news doesn't want to commit, attribution is everything. These openers shift responsibility to a source — useful for rumors and unconfirmed reports.

rows.source: Al parecer, el accidente fue grave.
Se rumorea que el gobierno dimitirá.

topics.title: Formal Spanish
topics.description: Usted, polite shifts, letters and emails, formal connectors

guide.intro: Formal Spanish lives in business emails, customer-service calls, official letters, and any context where you'd use 'usted' in English-as-Spanish. The hallmarks: 'usted', conditional softeners ('podría', 'sería tan amable'), fixed opening/closing formulas, and a leaner sentence rhythm.

sections.text: Salutations and closings
Letters and emails follow predictable patterns. Open formally, sign off warmly but professionally.
Polite verb shifts
Replace 'puedo', 'quiero', 'necesito' with softer forms — 'podría', 'quisiera', 'le agradecería que…' These signal respect and distance.

rows.translation: Could you send me the contract, please?

rows.source: Quisiera concertar una reunión con usted.
rows.translation: I'd like to arrange a meeting with you.

rows.source: Le agradecería que me confirmara la cita.
rows.translation: I would be grateful if you'd confirm the appointment.

sections.text: Usted vs tú

Use 'usted' (and 'ustedes' in plural) for clients, strangers in formal settings, older people, anyone you don't know well. In Spain, 'tú' has expanded — even between strangers under 40 — but business correspondence stays with 'usted'. Latin America is generally more conservative.
Formal connectors

items: con respecto a — with respect to
cabe señalar que — it is worth noting

sections.text: When in doubt, default to 'usted'. Switching from 'usted' to 'tú' is easy if the relationship warms up — going the other direction is awkward.

topics.title: Relative clauses
topics.description: Que, el que/el cual, cuyo, donde, lo que; specifying vs explanatory

guide.intro: Relative clauses let you add info about a noun without starting a new sentence. The workhorse is 'que' (works for people and things), but B2 demands more: 'el que / la cual' (after prepositions or for clarity), 'cuyo' (whose), 'donde' (where), and a sharp ear for whether the clause needs commas or not.

sections.text: Specifying (no commas) vs explanatory (with commas)
Specifying ('defining') clauses narrow down which noun you mean — no commas. Explanatory ('non-defining') clauses add bonus info — commas required.

rows.source: El libro que compré ayer es interesante. (specifying — which book?)
rows.translation: The book I bought yesterday is interesting.

rows.source: Mi hermano, que vive en Madrid, viene mañana. (explanatory — extra info)
rows.translation: My brother, who lives in Madrid, is coming tomorrow.

sections.text: Que vs el que / el cual
After a preposition or when 'que' would be ambiguous, switch to 'el que / la que / los que / las que' (or the slightly more formal 'el cual / la cual'). They agree with the noun's gender and number.

rows.source: La amiga con la que viajo es de Bogotá.
rows.translation: The friend I'm traveling with is from Bogotá.

rows.source: El proyecto del que te hablé está aprobado.
rows.translation: The project I told you about has been approved.

rows.source: Habló con el director, el cual decidió ayudar.
rows.translation: He spoke with the director, who decided to help.

sections.text: Cuyo — whose
'Cuyo' agrees with the noun it MODIFIES (not the owner). It's formal — often replaced in speech with 'que su…'.

rows.source: El autor cuyo libro leí ganó el premio.
rows.translation: The author whose book I read won the prize.

rows.source: La señora cuyos hijos son tus amigos vive al lado.
rows.translation: The lady whose kids are your friends lives next door.

sections.text: Donde — where
'Donde' replaces 'en el que / en la que' when referring to a place. Use 'a donde' for direction.

rows.source: La ciudad donde nací es muy pequeña.
rows.translation: The city where I was born is very small.

rows.source: El restaurante a donde vamos cierra a las 11.
rows.translation: The restaurant we're going to closes at 11.

sections.text: Spanish does NOT drop the relative pronoun like English does. 'The book I bought' must be 'el libro QUE compré', not 'el libro compré'.

items: el que / la que — the one that (clarifier)

topics.title: Modal perfects
topics.description: Should have, could have, must have — debería/podría/debe de haber + participle

guide.intro: Modal perfects — 'should have done', 'could have done', 'might have done' — pair a modal verb (deber, poder, tener que) with 'haber + participle'. They're the main way Spanish expresses past obligation, possibility, and missed-opportunity regret.

sections.text: Should have / shouldn't have
Use 'deber' (or 'tener que') in the conditional + 'haber + participle' for past obligation that wasn't met.
Could have
'Poder' (in conditional) + 'haber + participle' = 'could have'. Often used for missed opportunities or possibilities.

rows.translation: We could have gone to the cinema.
You could have told me sooner.

sections.text: Must have / may have (probability about the past)
'Deber de haber + participle' (or just conditional perfect 'habría…') expresses 'must have' / 'probably did'. 'Puede que haya + participle' expresses 'may have'.

rows.translation: It must have been a mistake.

sections.text: Word order tip: with reflexive/object pronouns, you can attach them to 'haber' or place them before 'debería' — 'Debería habérselo dicho' OR 'Se lo debería haber dicho'. Both correct.
Quick translation map

items: should have done — debería haber + participio
shouldn't have done — no debería haber + participio
could have done — podría haber + participio
must have done — debe de haber + participio / habrá + participio
might have done — puede que haya + participio

topics.title: Debate and disagreement
topics.description: Formal disagreement: discrepo, con todo respeto, aunque + subj., signposting

guide.intro: Formal disagreement in Spanish balances directness with respect. The key vocabulary: 'discrepo' (I disagree, formal), 'con todo respeto' (with all due respect), 'permítame discrepar' (allow me to differ), plus hedges, qualifiers, and signposts.

sections.text: Polite disagreement
Direct contradiction comes across as rude. Layer your dissent — acknowledge the other view, then introduce yours.

rows.source: Con todo respeto, no comparto esa opinión.
rows.translation: With all due respect, I don't share that opinion.

sections.text: Signposts for structuring a debate

items: En primer lugar… — In the first place…
Por otra parte… — On the other hand…
Cabe destacar que… — It's worth highlighting that…
Es preciso señalar que… — It must be pointed out that…
A modo de conclusión… — By way of conclusion…

sections.text: Hedge softeners

Even when sharp, Spanish debate softens with hedges like 'en cierta medida' (to some extent), 'hasta cierto punto' (up to a point), 'no del todo' (not entirely). They let you concede without conceding everything.

rows.source: Estoy de acuerdo hasta cierto punto.
rows.translation: I agree up to a point.

rows.source: Eso es cierto en cierta medida.

sections.text: Concession then pushback
The classic move: 'aunque + subjunctive, X is still true'. This lets you grant the opponent's point while resisting it.

rows.source: Aunque tenga razón en eso, sigo pensando que…
rows.translation: Even if you're right about that, I still think…

rows.source: Por más que insistas, no me convences.
rows.translation: However much you insist, you won't convince me.

topics.title: Indicative vs subjunctive with conjunctions
topics.description: Mood as meaning — aunque, cuando, donde, como, and porque swap moods to swap message

guide.intro: B2 is where Spanish mood stops being about triggers and starts being about meaning. The same conjunction (aunque, cuando, donde, como, porque) takes indicative or subjunctive depending on whether the event is real/known or hypothetical/unknown. Swapping the mood swaps the message.

sections.text: aunque — although vs even if
aunque + indicative = factual concession (the speaker treats the obstacle as real). aunque + subjunctive = hypothetical concession (the obstacle may or may not be real).

rows.translation: Although it's raining (and it IS), I'm going out.
Even if it rains, I'm going out.
Although it was expensive (and it was), we bought it.
Even if it were expensive, we'd buy it.

sections.text: cuando — habit, past, future-unknown
cuando + indicative = habit (present) or completed past. cuando + subjunctive = future event whose exact timing is unknown.

rows.translation: When he arrives (every night), we have dinner.
When he arrives (tonight), we'll have dinner.
When he arrived yesterday, we had dinner.

sections.text: donde / como — definite vs indefinite
donde and como with indicative point to a known place or specific manner. With subjunctive they mean 'wherever' or 'however' — indefinite.

rows.translation: I live where you were born. (specific known place)
Do it the way I taught you.

sections.text: porque and no porque
porque + indicative = real cause. no porque + subjunctive = denied cause, usually paired with 'sino porque + indicative' for the real one.

rows.translation: I'm staying because I want to.

rows.source: No me quedo porque sea fácil, sino porque me importa.
rows.translation: I'm not staying because it's easy, but because I care.

sections.text: Rule of thumb
If the speaker is asserting that the event happens (or happened, or always happens), use indicative. If the event is conditional, unknown, hypothetical, or being denied as a reason, use subjunctive.

topics.title: Conditional — politeness, hypothesis, hearsay
topics.description: One conjugation, three signals — court verbs, if-clause results, and Spanish news 'allegedly'

guide.intro: The Spanish conditional (-ría endings) is the same form for three completely different jobs. Recognizing which job is active is mostly a context skill — what's the sentence trying to do?

sections.text: 1. Politeness — softening requests, suggestions, opinions

Swap the present indicative for the conditional and your sentence loses its edge. 'Quiero un café' becomes 'Querría un café' (or even softer, 'Me gustaría un café'). Modal verbs (poder, deber, querer) and verbs of opinion (decir, pensar) take this softening especially well.

rows.translation: Could you help me for a moment?

rows.source: Yo diría que es buena idea.
rows.translation: I'd say it's a good idea.

sections.text: 2. Hypothetical — second-conditional result
Si + imperfect subjunctive in the if-clause, conditional in the main clause. Pure hypothetical: 'If I had X, I'd do Y.' Spanish never uses 'si + condicional' for this — that's a common mistake.

rows.translation: If I had time, I'd travel more.
What would you do if you were me?

sections.text: 3. Hearsay — Spanish news Spanish for 'allegedly'

Spanish journalism uses the conditional (often the conditional perfect 'habría + participle') to flag unconfirmed information. English needs 'allegedly' or 'reportedly'. Spot it by the news topic plus a source attribution like 'según fuentes', 'al parecer', 'fuentes indican'.

rows.source: El presidente habría declarado su apoyo.
rows.translation: The president allegedly declared his support.

rows.source: Según fuentes, los acusados habrían huido.
rows.translation: According to sources, the defendants allegedly fled.

rows.source: El alcalde estaría negociando un acuerdo.
rows.translation: The mayor is reportedly negotiating a deal. (present hearsay)

sections.text: How to tell them apart

Look at the surrounding clue: a polite phrase + modal verb? Politeness. A 'si + imperfect subjunctive' clause? Hypothesis. A news topic + 'según/al parecer/fuentes'? Hearsay. The conditional form is the same — context disambiguates.

sections.text: Quick reference — the B2 verb forms

rows.translation: after past triggers and in si-clauses (3rd cond.)

sections.text: Si-clause cheat sheet

items: Real: Si + present + present/future → 'Si llueve, no salgo'
Hypothetical (2nd cond.): Si + imperf. subj. + conditional → 'Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría'
Past unreal (3rd cond.): Si + plup. subj. + conditional perfect → 'Si hubiera sabido, habría venido'

sections.text: Indicative vs subjunctive after 'que'

items: Certainty / fact → indicative: 'Creo que es verdad', 'Es evidente que llueve'
Doubt / denial / emotion / influence → subjunctive: 'No creo que sea verdad', 'Es importante que estudies'
Past trigger → imperf. subj.: 'Quería que vinieras'

sections.text: When you're stuck, ask: am I expressing FACT or REACTION? Fact → indicative. Reaction (doubt, emotion, judgment, will) → subjunctive.

levels.name: C1 — Advanced
levels.description: Operate in Spanish for business, academic, and journalistic contexts. Argue a position, navigate Spain vs Latin American variants, and wield refranes and pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo with confidence.

topics.title: Spanish for business
topics.description: Meetings, negotiation, and formal proposals

guide.intro: Business Spanish lives a register above everyday speech. Where you'd say 'Te mando el contrato' to a friend, in a meeting you write 'Le adjunto el contrato para su revisión'. Three habits define the register: the formal 'usted/ustedes' and 'le/les', conditional softeners ('le agradeceríamos', 'sería conveniente'), and noun-heavy phrasing ('llevar a cabo una revisión' over 'revisar').

sections.text: Conditional softeners — agradeceríamos, convendría

Spanish business email leans hard on the conditional to soften requests. 'Le agradeceríamos que…' ('We would be grateful if you…') replaces a blunt imperative. 'Convendría revisar' ('It would be advisable to review') replaces 'tenemos que revisar'. The verb is conditional ('-ría'), and the subordinate clause goes into subjunctive ('que nos enviara').

rows.source: Le agradeceríamos que nos enviara la propuesta antes del viernes.
rows.translation: We would be grateful if you could send us the proposal before Friday.

rows.source: Convendría celebrar una reunión para tratar el asunto.
rows.translation: It would be advisable to hold a meeting to address the matter.

rows.source: Estaríamos encantados de recibir su confirmación.
rows.translation: We would be delighted to receive your confirmation.

sections.text: Formal salutations — estimado, distinguido

Open a business letter with 'Estimado/a' ('Dear') plus title and surname: 'Estimado Sr. García', 'Estimada Dra. Pérez'. For very senior audiences, 'Distinguido/a' bumps the formality further. Plurals: 'Estimados socios', 'Distinguidos accionistas'. Close with 'Reciba un cordial saludo' or the very formal 'Le saluda atentamente'.
Nominalization — llevar a cabo, hacer hincapié

Business Spanish prefers verb + noun collocations over single verbs. 'Llevar a cabo un análisis' ('carry out an analysis') sounds more polished than 'analizar'. 'Hacer hincapié en' ('emphasize') replaces 'subrayar'. 'Poner en marcha' ('launch') replaces 'empezar'. These collocations are fixed — swapping the verb breaks them.

rows.source: Hemos llevado a cabo una revisión exhaustiva del contrato.
rows.translation: We have carried out a thorough review of the contract.

rows.source: Quisiéramos hacer hincapié en los plazos de entrega.
rows.translation: We would like to emphasize the delivery deadlines.

rows.source: Pondremos en marcha el proyecto el próximo trimestre.
rows.translation: We will launch the project next quarter.

sections.text: Mixing registers stings. Once you open with 'Estimados socios', stay formal: keep 'ustedes', swap 'pero' for 'no obstante', and replace 'queremos' with 'desearíamos'.

topics.title: Academic discourse
topics.description: Lectures, papers, citations, and hedging

guide.intro: Academic Spanish is dense, hedged, and impersonal. Three habits set it apart from everyday speech: passive 'se' constructions to depersonalize ('se considera que', 'cabría señalar que'), conditional verbs for hedging ('podría argumentarse que'), and noun-heavy phrasing where English would use a verb ('llevar a cabo un análisis' rather than 'analizar').

sections.text: Impersonal 'se' — se considera, se desprende

Academic Spanish prefers impersonal constructions over 'yo creo'. 'Se considera que…' ('it is considered that…'), 'Se desprende que…' ('it follows that…'), and 'Cabe señalar que…' ('it is worth noting that…') let you make a claim without putting yourself forward. The construction is always third-person singular with 'se' before the verb.

rows.source: Se considera que este modelo es el más adecuado.
rows.translation: This model is considered to be the most appropriate.

rows.source: De los datos se desprende que la hipótesis es válida.
rows.translation: From the data it follows that the hypothesis is valid.

rows.source: Cabe señalar que el estudio presenta limitaciones.
rows.translation: It is worth noting that the study has limitations.

sections.text: Hedging — podría, cabría, parecería

Spanish academic prose hedges with the conditional ('-ría'). 'Podría argüirse que…' ('it could be argued that…'), 'Cabría destacar que…' ('it would be worth highlighting that…'), and 'Parecería que…' ('it would seem that…') soften any claim. Stack hedges to be more cautious.
Citations and attribution

Spanish academic writing uses 'según + author' (according to), 'siguiendo a + author' (following), and 'de acuerdo con' (in accordance with). For paraphrase: 'Como sostiene García (2020)…' ('As García maintains…'). For direct quote: 'En palabras de…' ('In the words of…').

rows.source: Según García (2020), el fenómeno tiene raíces sociales profundas.
rows.translation: According to García (2020), the phenomenon has deep social roots.

rows.source: Siguiendo a Pérez, podemos distinguir tres categorías.
rows.translation: Following Pérez, we can distinguish three categories.

rows.source: En palabras de la autora, 'el modelo es inadecuado'.
rows.translation: In the words of the author, 'the model is inadequate'.

sections.text: Mixing 'yo creo' into academic prose breaks register instantly. Replace 'yo creo que X' with 'cabría sostener que X' or 'se considera que X'.

lessons.title: Hedging claims

exercises.prompt: Which is the most academic way to introduce a hedged claim?
options: Yo creo que el modelo es bueno
Cabría argumentar que el modelo presenta ventajas
exercises.answer: Cabría argumentar que el modelo presenta ventajas
exercises.explanation: 'Cabría argumentar' (it could be argued) + 'presenta ventajas' (presents advantages) is the academic hedged register.

exercises.prompt: Complete the hedge: 'De los datos se ___ que el efecto es significativo' (it follows)
exercises.explanation: 'Se desprende que' = 'it follows that' — academic conclusion phrase.

exercises.prompt: the academic phrase to its function

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriately hedged for an academic abstract?
options: Los resultados parecerían sugerir que existe correlación
Los datos demuestran sin lugar a dudas la correlación
Salieron los números y hay relación
exercises.answer: Los resultados parecerían sugerir que existe correlación
exercises.explanation: 'Parecerían sugerir' double-hedges (would seem + suggest), proper for an abstract. The 'sin lugar a dudas' option is too strong; the others are colloquial.

exercises.prompt: 'No ___ que afirmar que la relación es causal' (one cannot)
exercises.explanation: 'No cabe afirmar' = 'one cannot claim'. 'Cabe / no cabe' is the academic 'fits / does not fit'.

options: Cabría sostener que el modelo es viable
Yo creo que el modelo es viable
Pienso que el modelo está bien
exercises.answer: Cabría sostener que el modelo es viable
exercises.explanation: 'Cabría sostener' is the formal academic hedge; the others are personal opinion phrasing.

exercises.prompt: What does 'sin pretender ser exhaustivos' mean in an academic intro?
exercises.explanation: 'Sin pretender' = 'without claiming/pretending to'. Standard academic disclaimer before a literature review.

exercises.prompt: 'Los resultados ___ apuntar a una posible correlación' (would seem to)
exercises.explanation: 'Parecerían apuntar' = 'would seem to point to' — conditional + infinitive academic hedge.

exercises.prompt: Spot the register mismatch in this academic sentence:

Conviene precisar que el estudio tiene limitaciones
exercises.answer: Pues el estudio tiene sus fallos, qué le vamos a hacer
exercises.explanation: 'Pues...qué le vamos a hacer' is colloquial. The other three stay in academic register.

lessons.title: Citing sources

Yo y García pensamos lo mismo
exercises.answer: Según García (2020), la teoría es incompleta
exercises.explanation: 'Según + author + (year)' is the standard academic citation framework.

exercises.prompt: '___ Pérez, podemos distinguir tres categorías' (Following)

exercises.answer: Según investigaciones recientes , el resultado es consistente

exercises.prompt: Which is the most academic way to introduce a counter-citation?

exercises.answer: En sentido contrario, Pérez (2019) sostiene que…
exercises.explanation: 'En sentido contrario' (in the opposite direction) is the academic register for introducing a counter-view.

topics.title: Society and public discourse
topics.description: Inequality, the welfare state, and public policy

guide.intro: Spanish public discourse has a vocabulary of its own. 'Brecha salarial', 'estado del bienestar', 'desigualdad social' are everyday tokens in op-eds and parliamentary debate. The register lives between academic prose and journalism — formal but accessible. Master the connectors ('cabe preguntarse si', 'es preciso reconocer') and the noun stock to read El País or La Nación with confidence.

sections.text: Core vocabulary — desigualdad, bienestar, derechos

Spanish public discourse repeats a tight set of nouns: 'desigualdad' (inequality), 'brecha' (gap), 'bienestar' (welfare/wellbeing), 'derechos' (rights), 'cohesión social' (social cohesion). The collocations are fixed: 'brecha salarial' (wage gap), 'brecha digital' (digital divide), 'cohesión territorial' (territorial cohesion). Learn the phrases, not just the words.

rows.source: La brecha salarial entre hombres y mujeres se ha reducido.
rows.translation: The wage gap between men and women has narrowed.

rows.source: El estado del bienestar requiere una financiación sostenible.
rows.translation: The welfare state requires sustainable financing.

rows.source: La cohesión social es uno de los pilares del modelo europeo.
rows.translation: Social cohesion is one of the pillars of the European model.

sections.text: Policy verbs — fomentar, impulsar, abordar

Public-policy Spanish uses a specific verb set. 'Fomentar' (foster), 'impulsar' (drive forward), 'abordar' (tackle), 'paliar' (alleviate), 'erradicar' (eradicate). These verbs almost always take noun-phrase objects: 'fomentar la igualdad', 'abordar la pobreza', 'paliar los efectos'.
Rhetorical questions — cabe preguntarse

Op-eds love the rhetorical question. 'Cabe preguntarse si…' ('one might ask whether…'), '¿Hasta qué punto…?' ('to what extent…'), '¿No sería preferible…?' ('would it not be preferable…') frame an argument by inviting the reader to consider an alternative.

rows.source: Cabe preguntarse si las políticas actuales bastan para revertir la tendencia.
rows.translation: One might ask whether current policies are enough to reverse the trend.

rows.source: ¿Hasta qué punto el modelo es sostenible?
rows.translation: To what extent is the model sustainable?
Would it not be preferable to invest in prevention?

sections.text: Public-discourse Spanish leans on nouns. Where English says 'we must protect workers', Spanish says 'es preciso garantizar la protección de los trabajadores'. The shift to nouns + 'es preciso/necesario' instantly raises the register.

topics.title: Refranes and modismos
topics.description: Spanish idioms — never translate literally

guide.intro: Spanish refranes (proverbs) and modismos (idioms) carry centuries of folk wisdom and emotional color. They almost never translate literally: 'costar un ojo de la cara' means 'to cost an arm and a leg', not 'to cost an eye of the face'. C1 mastery means recognizing these in conversation, choosing the right register, and avoiding word-for-word translation traps from English.

sections.text: Body-part idioms — un ojo de la cara, no pegar ojo

Spanish idiom-builds heavily off the body. 'Costar un ojo de la cara' (to cost an arm and a leg), 'no pegar ojo' (not sleep a wink), 'estar hasta las narices' (be fed up), 'meter la pata' (put your foot in it), 'tomar el pelo a alguien' (pull someone's leg). The verb is fixed — you can't swap 'costar' for 'valer' here.

rows.source: Ese coche cuesta un ojo de la cara.
rows.translation: That car costs an arm and a leg.

rows.source: Anoche no pegué ojo por el ruido.
rows.translation: Last night I didn't sleep a wink because of the noise.

rows.source: Estoy hasta las narices de esperar.
Metí la pata en la reunión.
rows.translation: I put my foot in it at the meeting.

sections.text: Animal idioms — gato, cabra, perro

Animals carry attitudes in Spanish idiom. 'Estar como una cabra' (be crazy, lit. 'be like a goat'), 'dar gato por liebre' (to swindle, lit. 'give cat for hare'), 'ser un lince' (be sharp, lit. 'be a lynx'), 'a otro perro con ese hueso' (tell that to someone else, lit. 'to another dog with that bone'). Native speakers reach for these constantly.
Action idioms — tirar la toalla, ponerse las pilas

Highly productive in everyday speech: 'tirar la toalla' (throw in the towel — give up), 'ponerse las pilas' (put your batteries in — get your act together), 'echar una mano' (lend a hand), 'hacer la vista gorda' (look the other way), 'estar en las nubes' (have your head in the clouds). These are register-neutral — you can use them with your boss or a friend.

rows.source: Después de tantos intentos, decidió tirar la toalla.
rows.translation: After so many attempts, he decided to throw in the towel.

rows.source: Si quieres aprobar, tienes que ponerte las pilas.
rows.translation: If you want to pass, you need to get your act together.

rows.source: ¿Me echas una mano con la mudanza?
rows.translation: Can you lend me a hand with the move?

sections.text: Two traps for English speakers: (1) Don't translate the English idiom directly — 'it's raining cats and dogs' is 'llueve a cántaros' in Spanish, not 'llueve gatos y perros'. (2) Watch for register: 'estar como una cabra' is fine with friends but odd in a formal report. Match the idiom to the situation.

topics.title: Advanced grammar
topics.description: Pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo, cleft 'lo que', advanced relatives

guide.intro: Four high-leverage C1 structures separate intermediate from advanced Spanish: the pluscuamperfecto del subjuntivo ('hubiera/hubiese' + participle) for past unreal conditions; cleft 'lo que' constructions for emphasis; advanced relative pronouns ('cuyo', 'el cual'); and stylistic inversion. Each construction signals literary or formal register and is essential for writing op-eds, essays, and well-spoken arguments.

sections.text: Pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo — hubiera / hubiese

For past unreal conditions ('if I had known…'), Spanish uses 'si + hubiera/hubiese + participle' in the if-clause, and 'habría + participle' (or 'hubiera + participle') in the main clause. 'Hubiera' and 'hubiese' are interchangeable; 'hubiera' is more common in Latin America, 'hubiese' in Spain — but both are correct everywhere.

rows.source: Si hubiera sabido la verdad, no habría venido.
rows.translation: If I had known the truth, I wouldn't have come.

rows.source: Si hubieses estudiado más, habrías aprobado.
rows.translation: If you had studied more, you would have passed.

rows.source: De haberlo sabido antes, hubiera reaccionado distinto.
rows.translation: Had I known earlier, I would have reacted differently.

sections.text: Cleft 'lo que' — emphasis structures

Cleft 'lo que' moves a constituent to the front for emphasis. 'Lo que pasa es que…' ('the thing is…'), 'Lo que más me gusta es…' ('what I like most is…'), 'Lo que necesitamos es tiempo' ('what we need is time'). The structure: 'lo que' + clause + 'es/son' + emphasized item.

rows.source: Lo que pasa es que no tenemos tiempo.
rows.translation: The thing is, we don't have time.

rows.source: Lo que más me sorprendió fue su reacción.
rows.translation: What surprised me most was his reaction.

rows.source: Lo que necesitamos es una solución integral.
rows.translation: What we need is a comprehensive solution.

sections.text: Advanced relatives — cuyo, el cual

Two relative pronouns belong only to C1+. 'Cuyo/a/os/as' = whose; it agrees with the noun that follows, not the antecedent: 'la mujer cuyos hijos…' ('the woman whose children…'). 'El cual / la cual / los cuales / las cuales' replaces 'que' in formal writing after prepositions, especially long ones: 'el problema sobre el cual hablamos' ('the problem about which we spoke').

rows: El motivo por el cual vine
Los temas sobre los cuales debatimos
El director, quien firmó el contrato

sections.text: Common trap: 'cuyo' agrees with the noun it modifies, not its antecedent. 'La empresa cuyos empleados' (the company whose employees) — 'cuyos' is masculine plural because it agrees with 'empleados', not feminine 'empresa'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'Si ___ sabido, no habría venido' (If I had known)
